title: Tarski’s exponential function problem
formal: Is the first-order theory of the standard real exponential field \(\mathbb R_{\exp}=(\mathbb R;0,1,+,-,\times,<,\exp)\) decidable? Precisely, does there exist one ordinary deterministic Turing machine \(D\) which halts on every encoded first-order sentence \(\varphi\) in this fixed language and outputs \(1\) exactly when \(\mathbb R_{\exp}\models\varphi\), and \(0\) otherwise? The exponential function is defined on all real numbers, and the required conclusion is unconditional.
definitions: The domain is the standard field \(\mathbb R\), with its usual constants, addition, unary additive inverse, multiplication and strict order. Equality is a logical symbol. Here \(\exp(x)=\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}x^j/j!\), the standard real exponential, with \(0!=1\); it is not an input function or an oracle available to the machine. Terms are finite expressions formed from variables \(v_i\), \(i\in\mathbb N=\{0,1,\ldots\}\), the constants \(0,1\), unary negation and exponentiation, and binary addition and multiplication. Atomic formulas are term equalities or strict inequalities. Formulas are formed using negation, conjunction, disjunction and the quantifiers \(\exists v_i\) and \(\forall v_i\). Every quantifier ranges over all of \(\mathbb R\), regardless of the index \(i\); indices name variables, not integer-valued inputs. Binding has its usual nested scope, with the nearest enclosing quantifier on a given variable binding that occurrence. A sentence is a formula with no free variables, and truth uses the ordinary real operations and ordinary first-order semantics. Arbitrarily many variables, nested exponentials and arbitrary finite quantifier alternations are allowed. There are no names for arbitrary real parameters, integer predicates, trigonometric functions or additional input operations. For a fixed finite-alphabet encoding, write a variable as v[b], where b is the usual binary expansion of its nonnegative index, with no leading zero except for the index zero itself. Use literal strings 0 and 1 for constants, and the prefix term forms -(t), exp(t), +(t,u) and *(t,u). Formula forms are =(t,u), <(t,u), not(phi), and(phi,psi), or(phi,psi), exists(v[b],phi) and forall(v[b],phi), with the indicated parentheses and commas and no spaces; t,u stand for terms and phi,psi for formulas, not literal tokens. Thus all inputs are finite strings over a fixed finite alphabet of these characters. To make D total on all strings, malformed encodings and formulas with free variables must be rejected with output 0. D has finite control and finitely many ordinary work tapes, has no oracle, noncomputable real constant, advice or random choices, and is the same machine for every input length, number of variables and quantifier pattern. No running-time or space upper bound is imposed beyond halting.
answer_criterion: Supply a complete, mathematically correct proof checked in Lean that such a single total deterministic Turing machine exists and has the stated exact truth behavior, or a complete Lean-checked proof that the language of true encoded sentences is undecidable by ordinary Turing machines. In the positive direction, termination and correctness must hold for every finite input, with the stated rejection convention on invalid strings. In the negative direction, the proof must rule out every candidate total decider, not merely refute one proposed algorithm or one recursively specified axiom system. A computably equivalent precise syntax may be used if its effective correspondence with the card’s encoding and sentence semantics is proved. A procedure that is correct whenever it terminates but lacks a universal termination proof does not meet the positive criterion. Deciding only a syntactic fragment qualifies only if the proof also establishes decidability of the full stated theory. Neither assuming Schanuel’s conjecture nor assuming another unresolved hypothesis is an unconditional resolution; the hypothesis would itself have to be proved in the accepted Lean development. Numerical evaluation with any fixed precision, bounded search for real solutions, or a time-complexity lower bound does not replace this exact decidability target.
why: A central boundary in exact algorithmic reasoning over real numbers: polynomial real arithmetic is decidable, while adding one standard analytic function connects logical truth to unresolved transcendence questions. Its resolution would determine whether a uniform symbolic decision procedure can handle all finite first-order specifications involving real exponentiation, with consequences for verification problems already reducible to this theory.

importance.reason: A longstanding central question of real model theory with direct relevance to symbolic reasoning about exponential expressions. The explicit 2026 conditional result confirms continuing specialist interest without settling the unconditional target.

progress.text: Tarski’s published decision theorem for polynomial real arithmetic establishes the starting point; the exponential extension is the further question described in the checked later primary literature.

Wilkie proves model completeness, and Macintyre–Wilkie prove decidability subject to the real Schanuel conjecture. The conditional result is described directly in Wilkie’s 1997 exposition and reviewed with exact hypothesis distinctions in the later sources.
The CONCUR weighted-automata paper invokes decidability of real-exponential arithmetic to obtain its bounded-language comparison result conditional on Schanuel’s conjecture.

The publisher releases the algorithmic-applications survey online, in a volume carrying a 2026 citation year. Section 3.1 distinguishes the stronger transcendence assumption from the weaker effective separation property equivalent to decidability.

context_blocks.text: Tarski’s decision theorem covers polynomial equations and inequalities over the reals with arbitrary first-order quantifiers. Adding the single function \(\exp\) asks whether that global decidability survives beyond polynomial arithmetic. The input remains a finite symbolic formula: a quantified real is part of the semantics, not a real number that must somehow be supplied as an infinite input string.

The target includes exact equalities and unrestricted quantifier alternation. For example, \(\forall x\,(x>0\Rightarrow\exists y\,\exp(y)=x)\) expresses surjectivity onto the positive reals; the implication here is an abbreviation for a disjunction in the specified syntax. Individual familiar identities are decidable, but they do not supply a machine for every sentence. Approximating an exponential value is also a different task: arbitrarily accurate approximations need not by themselves decide whether a given expression is exactly zero.

Wilkie proved model completeness of the real exponential theory in 1996: every formula is equivalent, in that theory, to an existential formula. The structure is also o-minimal, meaning that every definable subset of the real line is a finite union of points and intervals. These are strong finiteness properties, but neither statement alone certifies an algorithm for exact truth. The June 2026 paper recalls both results and distinguishes model completeness from completeness and effective axiomatization.

Macintyre and Wilkie proved decidability assuming the real form of Schanuel’s conjecture. That hypothesis says that whenever \(a_1,\ldots,a_n\in\mathbb R\) are linearly independent over \(\mathbb Q\), the field \(\mathbb Q(a_1,\ldots,a_n,\exp(a_1),\ldots,\exp(a_n))\) has transcendence degree at least \(n\) over \(\mathbb Q\). Linear independence means that a rational linear combination is zero only when every coefficient is zero; transcendence degree is the maximum number of elements algebraically independent over \(\mathbb Q\), meaning that no nonzero rational polynomial in those elements vanishes. Wilkie’s 1997 exposition explicitly describes the decidability result as conditional. The stronger conjecture about complex tuples is not required for this real-theory implication.

The algorithmic survey distinguishes Schanuel’s transcendence conjecture from a weaker effective separation statement equivalent to decidability. For integer polynomials \(p,q_1,\ldots,q_n\) in \(2n\) variables, set \(F_p(x)=p(x_1,\ldots,x_n,\exp(x_1),\ldots,\exp(x_n))\), and define \(F_{q_i}\) similarly. The weak statement asks for a computable positive integer \(\eta\) such that every common zero \(\gamma\) of the \(F_{q_i}\) with invertible derivative matrix \((\partial F_{q_i}/\partial x_j)(\gamma)\) satisfies \(|F_p(\gamma)|\leq1/\eta\Rightarrow F_p(\gamma)=0\). The source explains that some such separation value exists; the unresolved requirement is its uniform computability. Consequently, failure of the stronger Schanuel conjecture would not by itself establish undecidability.

Berarducci and Gallinaro’s revision of 23 June 2026 gives a new axiomatization of the full real exponential theory under the real Schanuel hypothesis. Its unconditional theorem concerns model completeness for axioms of a restricted exponential function: this function equals \(\exp(x)\) on \((-1,1)\) and zero outside that interval. Completeness for their axiom systems, including the unrestricted exponential system, still uses the conjecture. Thus the unconditional theorem is not an unconditional decision procedure for the full language on this card.

One application comes from weighted automata assigning nonnegative rational values to finite words. The CONCUR 2020 source asks whether two initial states define functions \(f,g\) with \(f(w)\leq Cg(w)\) for every word \(w\) and some constant \(C>0\). The general problem is undecidable, but when both positive-weight languages are bounded—each contained in a product \(w_1^*\cdots w_k^*\) of repetitions of finitely many fixed words—the source reduces the comparison to real-exponential arithmetic and obtains conditional decidability. Decidability of the present card would make that application unconditional; the unrelated undecidability result for arbitrary automata does not refute this theory’s decidability.

sentences: Tarski’s exponential function problem asks whether one terminating algorithm can decide every first-order sentence about the standard real numbers with their full exponential function.
The input is finite symbolic syntax with no arbitrary real constants or real-number oracle, and quantifiers range over all reals.
Acceptance requires a complete Lean-checked proof of total correct decidability or a proof of undecidability, with no time bound and no unresolved extra hypothesis.
The question extends decidable polynomial real arithmetic and already controls conditional verification results for restricted weighted automata.
Macintyre–Wilkie’s conditional theorem and the checked June2026 axiomatization still rely on the real Schanuel hypothesis; restricted model completeness is a different conclusion.
